topology: PC1 192.168.10.10/24 and PC2 192.168.10.20/24 connect through SW1 to R1 Gi0/0 192.168.10.1/24. PC3 192.168.40.10/24 connects to R1 Gi0/3 192.168.40.1/24. R1 Gi0/1 192.168.20.1/24 connects to protected SRV1 192.168.20.10/24; Gi0/2 192.168.30.1/24 connects to control SRV2 192.168.30.10/24. All hosts have gateways; both servers have HTTP ready.
verificationNotes: Practice begins at zero credit. The completed reference configures only R1 and earns two live configuration goals, with no packet evidence preloaded. Five ping checks and three HTTP checks supply the eight traffic achievements.

Named standard ACL SERVER-ACCESS permits host 192.168.10.10 at sequence10 and denies source subnet 192.168.10.0/24 at sequence20. PC2 matches the explicit subnet deny; PC3 is denied implicitly. Standard filtering is source-only and the /24 wildcard is 0.0.0.255.

The ACL is applied only outbound on R1 Gi0/1 near protected SRV1. The live binding check requires operational placement and no extra IPv4 interface bindings. Denied PCs must still reach unfiltered SRV2, distinguishing selective access control from broad connectivity loss.

Bounded, secret-free runtime ACL decisions record only actual applied interface filtering, including packet identity, direction, rule sequence or implicit decision, and TCP transaction. Advisory ACL queries and NAT/QoS classifier calls cannot create packet-filter proof. Existing permit/deny logic and IOS counters are preserved.

Permitted ICMP requires a corresponding interface permit, destination request acceptance and successful return. Denial requires the intended interface decision and the matching real drop. A powered-off endpoint, wrong direction, missing route, unrelated drop or raised hit counter cannot finish it.

HTTP permits require complete client/server delivery with the expected page and applied request permit. Blocked HTTP requires the actual SYN transaction and intended explicit/implicit drop, rather than a generic HTTP failure.

Counter checks distinguish sequence10 permit, sequence20 deny and implicit deny. Clearing counters changes neither policy nor achievements; implicit denial does not create a visible ACE or explicit sequence counter.

Wrong placement on the shared source LAN also cuts PC2 off from the control server. Wrong direction filters server responses instead of proving the intended client-source restriction. Missing host permit lets the broader subnet deny match PC1. Repairs and all published verification commands are tested.

Achieved packet tasks survive portable saves and browser reopening, while policy and binding remain live. Fresh runtime counters and decision evidence are rebuilt after load. The catalog and guide use the existing offline simulator and do not claim new live CML validation.
